← Overview Two regional examples / nothing added on top

Plain arepas, side by side

Both use maize, water, and salt. One starts with dried, dehulled kernels that are soaked, cooked, and ground; the other starts with precooked maize flour. Make and serve them plain to see what the preparation itself contributes.

These are two documented recipes, not rules for every arepa in Colombia or Venezuela. Neither card adds cheese, butter, oil, a filling, or a topping.

Colombia / Antioquia

Arepa antioqueña

A kernel-to-dough route: soften dehulled maize, grind a smooth dough, then roast it golden. This version follows Fundación Secretos para Contar’s Del campo a la mesa recipe.

Makes 10Overnight soak + cooking, grinding, and griddling; the source gives no exact cook time.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups dried maíz trillado (dehulled maize)
  • 3 L water for cooking the soaked grain, then drained
  • Salt to taste
  • Additional water to cover the grain while soaking

Method

  1. Cover the maize with water and soak overnight. Drain.
  2. Cook in the 3 L of fresh water until the grain is between hard and very soft: tender enough to grind, but not mushy. Drain and let cool.
  3. Grind finely into a smooth dough. Knead in salt. Divide into 10 and shape into rounds. We choose thin rounds, one of several Antioquian shapes described by Colombia’s Ministry of Culture; the Fundación recipe does not set a thickness.
  4. Roast on a hot cooking surface, turning so both sides become golden. A griddle or skillet is a practical home substitute. Serve plain.
At the finish

The source asks for a very smooth ground-grain dough and golden faces. It gives no fixed diameter or number of minutes on the griddle.

Recipe: Fundación Secretos para Contar, p. 92 ↗ · Shape option: Colombia Ministry of Culture, pp. 265–266 ↗

Venezuela / precooked-flour version

Arepa venezolana tradicional

A flour route: hydrate precooked white maize flour, rest briefly, form discs, and griddle. The three-ingredient formula comes from P.A.N.’s published recipe.

Makes 8–101–2 minutes kneading, 3–5 minutes resting, then about 5 minutes per side.

Ingredients

  • 2 cups P.A.N. precooked white maize flour
  • 2½ cups water, mixed into the dough
  • 1 tsp salt

Method

  1. Stir the salt into the water. Add the precooked flour gradually.
  2. Knead for 1–2 minutes until smooth; let the dough rest for 3–5 minutes.
  3. Divide into 8–10 equal portions, roll into balls, and flatten with your palms into discs about 10–12 cm (4–5 in) across.
  4. Cook on a griddle or skillet over medium heat for about 5 minutes on each side. Serve the rounds plain, without cutting or filling them.
At the finish

The source specifies a smooth dough, the disc diameter, and a measured time on each face. It suggests opening the arepa for a filling afterward; this comparison stops before that step.

Recipe: P.A.N., traditional Venezuelan arepa ↗

The useful difference

What changes between these two recipes?

Read the quantities in context: Colombia’s 3 L is cooking water discarded before grinding. Venezuela’s 2½ cups becomes part of the dough. The comparison reflects the cited versions, not a countrywide divide.

FeatureAntioquian exampleVenezuelan example
Maize at the startDried, dehulled kernelsPrecooked white maize flour
Where the water goesSoak, then cook in 3 L; drain before grindingMix 2½ cups directly into 2 cups flour
Before shapingOvernight soak, cook, cool, grind, and kneadKnead 1–2 minutes; rest 3–5 minutes
Shape in these versionsThin round chosen from documented regional options; no fixed diameter8–10 rounds, about 10–12 cm across; no stated thickness
Heat and finish cueRoast both faces until golden; no fixed timeMedium griddle, about 5 minutes each side
As served herePlain, golden ground-maize arepaPlain, uncut precooked-flour arepa
What the sources do not settle

They do not measure the two finished textures in a controlled tasting. Grain variety, exact thickness, grinding, moisture, and heat can all change the bite. The Colombian regional survey itself records several maize and shape variations. This page compares two recipes, not two national definitions. Sources & credits

The two formulas and regional shape note are linked beside their claims; photographs have separate authorship and licenses.

  1. Fundación Secretos para Contar · Arepa antioqueña, Del campo a la mesa p. 92 ↗

    Original ten-arepa formula: two cups maíz trillado, three liters of cooking water, salt, overnight soak, cooking, grinding, and roasting to golden.

  2. Colombia Ministry of Culture · Paseo de olla, pp. 265–266 ↗

    Describes the range of Antioquian maize arepas and thin rounds as one shape for white maíz trillado. It does not set the Fundación recipe’s exact thickness.

  3. P.A.N. · Arepa venezolana tradicional ↗

    Published three-ingredient, 8–10 arepa method with flour-to-water ratio, dough rest, diameter, and griddle timing. Its subsequent filling step is omitted here.

  4. Eddy Milfort · Arepas (Itagüí) photograph ↗

    CC BY-SA 2.0; original photograph displayed with a crop that excludes filled arepas. Illustrative, not a photo of the cited recipe.

  5. Periodismodepaz · Arepas venezolanas photograph ↗

    CC BY-SA 4.0; illustrative unfilled arepas, not a photo of the cited recipe.
